questions.q: What is a "feature," as distinct from a neuron, in this lesson's terminology?
options: A feature and a neuron are exactly the same thing in every model
A specific, interpretable property a model represents, which may not correspond cleanly to any single neuron
A feature is only ever a single weight value
A feature is a term used exclusively in computer vision models, never in language models
questions.explain: Features are the interpretable concepts a model tracks; neurons are just activation-vector coordinates that don't necessarily map one-to-one onto those concepts.

questions.q: According to "Toy Models of Superposition," how can a model represent more features than it has dimensions?
options: It cannot -- the number of features is always capped at the number of dimensions
By assigning each feature its own direction and letting those directions be non-orthogonal/overlapping rather than perfectly separated
By deleting all but the most important feature
By increasing the model's vocabulary size
questions.explain: Superposition means packing feature directions close together rather than keeping them orthogonal, trading some interference for extra representational capacity.

questions.q: Why does sparsity make superposition a good trade-off rather than a disaster?
options: Sparsity has no relationship to superposition at all
Because only a small fraction of features are active on any given input, overlapping features rarely interfere with each other in practice
Because sparse features are always stored on separate, dedicated neurons
Because sparsity eliminates the need for any hidden dimensions
questions.explain: If two overlapping features are rarely both active at once, the interference between their shared direction barely shows up in practice, making the overlap cheap.

questions.q: In the lesson's toy-model code, why can't the columns of `W` all be mutually orthogonal?
options: Because `n_features` (20) is larger than `d_hidden` (5), so there isn't enough room in a 5-dimensional space for 20 mutually orthogonal directions
Because `torch.relu` makes orthogonality impossible by definition
Orthogonality is unrelated to the dimensions of `W`
Because the sparsity mask directly forces non-orthogonality
questions.explain: A `d_hidden`-dimensional space can hold at most `d_hidden` mutually orthogonal directions, so with more features than hidden dimensions, some overlap is unavoidable.

questions.q: Why are individual neurons often not directly interpretable, according to this lesson?
options: Because all neurons are randomly initialized and never trained
Because a neuron's activation can be a blend of contributions from several superposed features rather than a clean signal for just one
Because neurons only exist in the model's final layer
Because interpretability research has shown neurons carry no information whatsoever
questions.explain: Polysemantic neurons mix contributions from multiple overlapping feature directions, which is exactly what superposition predicts and what makes raw neuron activations hard to read.
